cards.title: Ubuntu still has not released patch for Linux 0day RCE in almost 3 weeks

depth.text: Ubuntu still hasn't shipped a **kernel fix** for a critical Linux flaw, leaving several LTS releases **exposed**

Ubuntu has no patched kernels for **22.04, 24.04, or 26.04**, despite the flaw's **CVSS 9.8** rating, and hasn't given an **ETA**. cards.title: We halved DNS build delay and cut memory use by 85%

cards.title: China's First Frontier AI Export Controls: Mofcom Announcement No. 48

depth.text: China is proposing **export controls** for frontier AI, while a **registration rule** already applies

The draft restricts **model weights** and know-how if a model meets any one of three tests: at least **10^26 FLOPs**, at least 2 trillion parameters, or a global top-10 position. A separate interim registration rule already covers certain transfers, including overseas licensing and changes of ownership or control; the draft is open for comment until November 15, 2026.

cards.camps: Two camps: one commenter fears restrictions will make powerful Chinese models hard to adopt; another points to China's stated support for open-source exports and the public-domain exemption.

comments.text: https://www.mofcom.gov.cn/xwfb/xwfyrth/art/2026/art_d7661dbf... "Second, we encourage open source, open collaboration, and resource sharing. The Chinese government is committed to making artificial intelligence a significant driving force for promoting common prosperity and safeguarding common security. To support the construction of an open source innovation ecosystem for artificial…

I understand why China wants to restrict exports of their models. But I feel the only reason Chinese models have been able to gain such popularity is BECAUSE they are open source. I wouldn’t trust models from China enough to use them in important work unless they were open. Restricting any powerful Chinese model [that ranks in the global top 10] is going to make them very difficult to advocate…
These rules are not new, right? They appear to match the previous guidance (restrictions on top-10 models, exemption for open-source collaboration)

The risk is that USA and China will come together on a joint "AI non-proliferation" agreement in the same way that nuclear technology became restricted by the countries that already had the capability. This will lead to a de facto techno-colonization of the rest of the world just between themselves. This was a topic of discussion at Trump and Xi's AI summit just last month. We're now starting to…

slightly ot, but this seems like a good place to ask, since I don't think I have the strategic-business mind to understand it all myself: What's the play here with China having supported publishing open weight models this far? I know the official line is for the good of mankind and all that, but presumably it's more strategic than that. Soft power? Commoditise your competition?

glossary.CVE: Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures: a standard ID assigned to a publicly known security flaw so people can refer to the same issue.
glossary.CVSS: Common Vulnerability Scoring System: a scale people use to rate how serious a security flaw is.
glossary.LTS: Long-term support: a release its makers promise to support for an extended period.
glossary.kernel: A small program that carries out a calculation on a computer's graphics chip or processor.
glossary.multi-tenant: A system used by several customers or groups, with each kept separate from the others.
glossary.out-of-tree mitigation: A workaround made outside the official project, rather than included in its standard updates.
glossary.RCE: Remote Code Execution: a flaw that lets an attacker make a computer run their commands from somewhere else.
glossary.IPO: Initial Public Offering: when a company first offers its shares for the public to buy.
glossary.SEC: Securities and Exchange Commission: the agency that oversees company filings for stock-market listings.
glossary.non-cancelable spending commitments: Payments a company has promised in a contract to make later, even if it would rather not.
glossary.registration statement: A document a company files before an IPO that lays out information about its business and finances.
glossary.audited financial statements: Company accounts checked by auditors to see whether the numbers are reliable.
glossary.index fund: A fund that owns a group of investments meant to track a particular market list.
glossary.NEV: New Energy Vehicle: a broad label for vehicles such as fully electric cars and plug-in hybrids.
glossary.PHEV: Plug-in hybrid vehicle: a car that can charge from a plug and also uses a fuel engine.
glossary.ICE: Internal Combustion Engine: an engine that makes power by burning fuel inside it.
glossary.DevOps: The work of getting software released and keeping it running.
glossary.fullstack: Building both the part people use and the behind-the-scenes part.
glossary.founding engineer: One of the first engineers at a new company.
glossary.sequential growth: Growth compared with the previous quarter.
glossary.annualized revenue run-rate: A way to show what a company's revenue would be over a full year if its current pace continued.
glossary.GUI: Graphical user interface: the buttons, pictures, and menus you use on a screen instead of typing commands.
glossary.microkernel: A small operating-system core that leaves many jobs to other parts of the system.
glossary.RAM: Random-Access Memory: a computer's working space for information it is using right now.
glossary.M.2 SSD: M.2 is a small plug-in shape; SSD means Solid-State Drive, a storage device that keeps files even when the computer is off.
glossary.systemd: A Linux tool that starts programs in the background and keeps track of them.
glossary.daily driver: The device someone uses regularly as their main one.
glossary.IPS: In-Plane Switching: a kind of screen that keeps colors looking more consistent when viewed from the side.
glossary.thin client: A simple device that mostly shows what another, more powerful computer is doing.
glossary.CPU: Central Processing Unit: the main chip that runs instructions in a computer.
glossary.GPU: Graphics Processing Unit: the chip part that draws images and video.
glossary.net worth: What you own minus what you owe.
glossary.median: The middle value when the results are put in order.
glossary.top 10%: The highest tenth of the group, at a level only one in ten people exceeds.
glossary.percentile: A way to divide a group ranked from lowest to highest into 100 equal-sized slices.
glossary.household-level: Numbers measured for a household, so a couple's finances are combined rather than counted person by person.
glossary.modeled estimate: A figure worked out from data using a model, rather than a direct count of every person.
glossary.microdata: Detailed records from a survey, rather than only its summarized results.
glossary.SCF: Survey of Consumer Finances: a Federal Reserve survey used as one source for these estimates.
glossary.market value: The total value of a company’s shares at their current prices.
glossary.share buybacks: When a company uses money to buy its own shares from investors.
glossary.midterm cycle: A stretch around elections held halfway through a US president’s term.
glossary.hyperscaler: A company that rents servers and computing power at huge scale.
glossary.senior notes: Company borrowing that gets paid before lower-priority borrowing if the company cannot repay all its debts.
glossary.free cash flow: Money a company has left after paying for its regular operations and other spending.
glossary.credit default swaps: A way to insure against a company failing to repay its debt.
glossary.dilution: When a company issues more shares, each existing share becomes a smaller part of the company.
glossary.vendor financing: A way for a supplier to help a customer pay for what it buys, often over time.
glossary.solopreneur: Someone who is the sole paid employee of their business.
glossary.cybersecurity: Steps for keeping computers, accounts and business information safe from attacks.
glossary.NIST Cybersecurity Framework: NIST guidance that helps businesses decide how to protect their computer systems and handle risks.
glossary.default password: A password already set on a device; owners should replace it because criminals may know it.
glossary.re-skin: A change to how a site looks that leaves its content or features mostly the same.
glossary.high-density design: A layout that fits more stories or other items into the same space.
glossary.DNS: Domain Name System: the internet's address book, which helps a computer find a website from its name.
glossary.zone: A separate part of a cloud provider’s setup; a problem in one zone may not affect services in other zones.
glossary.targeted build: A rebuild that handles only the names or settings a change can affect, instead of checking every record in the zone.
glossary.Kafka: A system Cloudflare uses to pass change messages between parts of its service.
glossary.Kafka partition: A group of Kafka messages kept in order; later messages cannot be confirmed until earlier ones are done.
glossary.Quicksilver: Cloudflare's storage system for DNS data, which it spreads across its network.
glossary.p99: The time within which 99% of measured events finished.
glossary.capex: Capital expenditure: money spent up front on equipment or building something.
glossary.H1B: A US work visa that lets employers hire some workers from abroad for specialized jobs.
glossary.offshoring: Moving work to another country instead of doing it where the company is based.
glossary.asynchronous work: Work people do at different times, rather than needing everyone to be online together.
glossary.equity: Ownership in a company, rather than lending it money.
glossary.Git: A tool for keeping a history of code changes and combining work.
glossary.source control: Tools for keeping track of changes to code and helping developers work on it together.
glossary.agent: An AI system that can take steps and use tools to get a task done, not just answer questions.
glossary.monorepo: One repository that holds code for many projects or services.
glossary.commit: A saved record of changes in a project; this site treats posts like commits.
glossary.DuckDB: A tool for analyzing data on one machine; it can keep working by using the computer’s storage when memory fills up.
glossary.DuckLake: A data format designed to work across different database setups.
glossary.Trino: A tool for asking questions of data stored in a warehouse.
glossary.HogLake: PostHog’s own open format for organizing tables in its warehouse.
glossary.lakehouse: A way to store lots of data while still making it easy to work with like a database.
glossary.catalog: A list of a warehouse’s tables and details about them.
glossary.snapshot: A saved state of a running virtual machine that can be started again later.
glossary.single-node: A setup where one machine does the work, rather than splitting it across several machines.
glossary.query optimizer: The part of a database that picks a way to answer a data question efficiently.
glossary.pgwire: The way Postgres apps communicate with a database over a network.
glossary.TTL: Time to live: how long a saved item or sign-in token stays valid.
glossary.fork: A separate copy of a shared software project that people can take in a different direction.
glossary.public relations: Work aimed at shaping how the public sees a person or group.
glossary.authorised biography: A book about someone written with their permission and cooperation.
glossary.stakeholders: People or groups with an interest in, or affected by, a decision.
glossary.frontier AI: The most capable AI systems being built at a particular time.
glossary.model weights: The learned settings inside an AI that shape how it responds.
glossary.FLOPs: Floating-point operations: a count of computer math steps, used here as a measure of how much compute a run takes.
glossary.export control: A government rule that limits sending certain goods or technology across borders.
glossary.open weights: The model's learned settings are available for people to download and run themselves.
